cards.front: “When I Have Fears That I May Cease to Be”
cards.back: John Keats (Romantics); a Shakespearean sonnet

cards.front: “When I Have Fears”: the speaker’s fear
cards.back: Dying before he writes his great works or fully experiences love
Agricultural simile (books as harvested grain); personified night looking down on him

cards.front: “When I Have Fears”: how the speaker changes
cards.back: From pride in his ambitions to fear, then acceptance of how small he is

cards.front: “When I Have Fears”: the most important part
cards.back: The opening: high hopes for his writing versus looming death
William Wordsworth (Romantics)

cards.front: “I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud”: main idea
cards.back: Nature, through personified dancing daffodils, is isolating yet empowering

cards.front: “I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud”: how the speaker changes
cards.back: Watches the daffodils, then dances with them, then recalls them for inspiration

cards.front: “Strange Fits of Passion Have I Known” (Lucy 1)
cards.back: William Wordsworth (Romantics); the first Lucy poem
Moon symbolism and visual imagery show how fear affects love

cards.front: Lucy 1: what the moon stands for
cards.back: His destination and the passage of time; it sinks as he nears Lucy

cards.front: Lucy 1: the ride to Lucy’s cottage
cards.back: Exciting but worrisome, and it feels endless
All quatrains: four lines each, echoing the four seasons and nature
Walt Whitman (Romantics on the sheet); free verse
Self-discovery in nature matters more than structured education
Matter-of-fact academic terms first, then free, mystical words like “rising”
Lines 1–4 repeat “When I” and feel fixed; shift at line 5; then open
Its open form mirrors learning through spirituality and personal enlightenment

cards.front: “Thirteen Ways of Looking at a Blackbird”
cards.back: Wallace Stevens (Modernists)
Thirteen viewpoints of one bird; Modernism favors many perspectives at once

cards.front: “Thirteen Ways”: the river and the blackbird
cards.back: Merges the bird with its environment, effacing individuality

cards.front: “Thirteen Ways”: golden birds vs. the blackbird
cards.back: People chase golden birds (unattainable goals) while the real blackbird is right there
Both reverent and unsettled
Langston Hughes (Harlem Renaissance)

cards.front: “Theme for English B”: why personify Harlem?
cards.back: Humanizing Harlem humanizes its people

cards.front: “Theme for English B”: why so many questions?
cards.back: Unsure he can speak for himself; questioning what being American means

cards.front: “Theme for English B”: the color of the page
cards.back: The paper is white; his color is what he adds to it

cards.front: “Theme for English B”: “Bessie, bop, or Bach”
cards.back: Bessie Smith and bebop are Black music, Bach is white European; tastes cross lines

cards.front: “Theme for English B”: speaker and instructor
cards.back: Part of each other, even when they don’t want to be connected
Sylvia Plath (Post-Modernists, Confessional)
Chaotic (especially stanza 2), then introspective

cards.front: “Blackberrying”: the hooks and turns toward the sea
cards.back: Changes in life
“Nothing” and “protesting”
Free verse, personal pronouns, innermost thoughts, rewritten prosody
Anne Sexton (Post-Modernists, Confessional)
Echoes the witch trials; her own experience of how women get labeled
Three stanzas, three types of women, each ending “I have been her kind”
Abstractly dark
